# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure that arises in previously healthy women toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery. The first formal case definition, established by a 2000 National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and Office of Rare Diseases workshop, required cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction [1]. Because women presenting before the final gestational month proved clinically indistinguishable from those meeting the strict temporal criteria, the 2010 Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group broadened the definition: PPCM was revised to an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to LV systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, where no other cause is found, with LVEF typically below 45% and the ventricle not necessarily dilated [2]. The 2019 HFA position statement reaffirmed PPCM as a diagnosis of exclusion requiring a high index of suspicion, since dyspnoea, fatigue and oedema are common in normal pregnancy [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography and ethnicity. It ranges from approximately 1 in 299 births in Haiti to about 1 in 1000 in South Africa and the USA, with much lower rates reported in parts of Europe [4]. In a US nationwide analysis, PPCM incidence was lowest in Hispanic women and highest in African American women, and the diagnosis has become more frequent over time [5]. Earlier US series likewise emphasised rising incidence and important regional and racial differences in presentation [6]. Established risk factors include African ancestry, advanced maternal age, multiple gestation, hypertensive disorders and pre-eclampsia [7].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but increasingly framed around hormonal and vascular mechanisms. A pivotal experimental study showed that female mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of STAT3 develop PPCM, with enhanced cardiac cathepsin D activity generating an antiangiogenic, proapoptotic 16-kDa form of prolactin; bromocriptine prevented disease, whereas forced myocardial generation of 16-kDa prolactin recapitulated the phenotype [8]. A broader review synthesised inflammation, autoimmunity, apoptosis, endothelial dysfunction and peripartum oxidative stress as contributing features, with prolactin cleavage as a unifying pathomechanism [9]. The 16-kDa fragment acts in part through microRNA-146a, identified as a therapeutic target and biomarker for PPCM [10]. A complementary "vascular" model demonstrated that PPCM is associated with systemic angiogenic imbalance accentuated by pre-eclampsia, with mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α developing profound PPCM that is rescued by pro-angiogenic therapy, while the placenta secretes anti-angiogenic sFLT1 [11]. A contemporary review further details the cascade linking oxidative stress, cathepsin D and prolactin in disease initiation [12].

## Genetics

PPCM shares a genetic architecture with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). In a landmark sequencing study, the prevalence of truncating variants (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population, two-thirds were in TTN, and almost all TTN variants localised to the titin A-band [13]. Notably, the presence of TTN truncating variants correlated with lower ejection fraction at one-year follow-up [13]. Truncating TTN variants are also the most common known genetic cause of DCM [14], and a multicentre study confirmed that approximately 10% of women with PPCM harbour TTN truncating variants, though whether mutations in other genes predispose to PPCM was previously unknown [15]. The ESC has noted that around 15–20% of patients carry cardiomyopathy-associated mutations in genes such as TTN, MYH7, MYBPC3, LMNA and SCN5A [3].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Patients typically present with HFrEF in the last month of pregnancy or postpartum. Measurement of natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography and echocardiography are recommended to diagnose or exclude PPCM, and important differential diagnoses include pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, hypertensive heart disease and pre-existing heart disease [3]. Comprehensive reviews underscore that PPCM remains a diagnosis of exclusion and that delays are common because symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy [6,16].

## Management

Treatment combines guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure—adapted for pregnancy and lactation—with attention to anticoagulation given the elevated thromboembolic risk [16]. Disease-specific therapy targeting prolactin has been the major therapeutic innovation. A proof-of-concept South African study found that bromocriptine-treated patients displayed greater recovery of LVEF (27% to 58%) than standard-care patients, and significantly fewer experienced the composite poor outcome of death, NYHA III/IV, or LVEF below 35% at six months [17]. A subsequent German multicentre randomised trial compared dosing regimens and reported that bromocriptine was associated with a high rate of full LV recovery and low morbidity and mortality, with no significant difference between one-week and eight-week treatment [18]. Meta-analyses suggest a benefit on LVEF when bromocriptine is added to standard therapy, though trials remain small and underpowered, and bromocriptine carries thromboembolic and lactation-related concerns [19,20].

## Outcomes

Recovery is frequent but variable. In the North American IPAC cohort, event-free survival at one year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and 72% of patients achieved an LVEF of 50% or greater at 12 months [21]. The first global ESC EORP registry enrolled women across 49 countries and found that just under half of deaths occurred within 30 days of diagnosis, just under half of women recovered within six months, and neonatal death occurred in 5% [22,23]. Subsequent pregnancies carry meaningful risk, particularly in women with incomplete recovery, as documented in US clinical characterisation and recent registry analyses [6,24]. Recent population-based registries continue to show increasing recognition of PPCM, with prognosis tied to baseline ventricular function [5]. Ongoing research into genetic, vascular and hormonal mechanisms is expected to refine risk stratification and disease-specific therapy [12,15].
